newsitem.title: USA: Key senator wary of power reliability legislation.
newsitem.headline: Key senator wary of power reliability legislation.

text.p: U.S. Senator Frank Murkowski, chairman of the Senate Energy Committee, said Thursday he was leery of any move to make voluntary electric reliability measures enforceable by federal law.

The Clinton administration is considering a plan to provide a legal backstop for industry rules for maintaining a reliable power grid, as states move to open local power markets to competition and draw new players into the business.
"This raises a host of very difficult and thorny questions," said Murkowski, an Alaska Republican.

"I will not allow reliability to become a backdoor means to preempt state control over electric utilities and to federalize the day-to-day operations of the electric industry," he said at a committee workshop on deregulation.
The industry had effectively managed to ensure steady supplies of power through voluntary standards, he said.

Making those standards enforceable by the federal government would require lawmakers to address difficult issues including the governance of the North American Electric Reliability Council, its jurisdiction, antitrust issues, and U.S. treaty relations with Canada and Mexico, he said.

However, the NERC itself said it might need some backup from the federal government, because reliability might become more difficult to control under a voluntary system with many new players getting into the electricity supply business.

"We think we need something more than what we have now," NERC vice president David Nevius said at the workshop. But he added, "We've been cautioned about asking for help (from Congress) because there are lots of unintended consequences."
